docs.title: pMHC-TCR MD and Free Energy Workflow Documentation
docs.text:
Documentation to deploy and use automated workflows for conformational simulations and free energy computations of pMHC-TCR proteins complexes using GROMACS and PyCOMPSs.

Start here: Quickstart Guide · Source code: GitHub Repository

This is part of the GANANA Life Science pillar (WP3) - Project 3 "Framework for AI-driven Immunogenic Peptide Prediction".

docs.title: How to contribute to the project
docs.text: There are two possible ways to exploit this repo. The first one is to fork, i.e. copy, this repo and use it as a template or starting point to generate your workflow. On the other hand, if you want to improve it, you can copy, modify it and then open a Pull Request to the original repo.

docs.title: Open issues
docs.text: If you find bugs or have feature requests, please open an issue. We provide templates to guide the process.

docs.title: Contribute to the code (a.k.a. open a Pull Request)
docs.text:
Info

This guide assumes that you are able to clone repositories from your GitHub account. One way to do this is by means of ssh keys, however other ways are possible.

To contribute code improvements or new features, follow these steps:

  1. Fork this repository to your GitHub account.
  2. Clone your fork locally: 
    git clone https://github.com/your-username/WP3-P3-md-workflow.git
  3. Create a new branch for your work: 
    git switch -c feat-branch-name
  4. Make your changes and commit them with clear messages: 
    git add -A
git commit -m "Describe your commit"
  5. Push your branch to your fork: 
    git push --set-upstream origin feat-branch-name
  6. Open a Pull Request (PR) to the main repo’s default branch.
  7. Wait for a review before merge.

docs.title: Python style
docs.text:
Python codes use the ruff formatter in its default configuration. Install ruff (once) and format before committing:

ruff format md/workflow/md.py

IDE integration: Most editors (VS Code, PyCharm, Neovim) support ruff natively through extensions.

docs.title: Contribute to the documentation
docs.text: Documentation is built with MkDocs using the Material theme and hosted on GitHub Pages. Documentation is built to be displayed both on GitHub and in an HTML form, hence graphical artifacts might be present.

docs.title: Preview locally
docs.text:
If using uv: 

uvx --with mkdocs-material mkdocs serve

otherwise

python -m venv .venv
. .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -r docs/requirements.txt

Then, open http://127.0.0.1:8000.

docs.title: Edit workflow
docs.text:
1. Edit .md files in docs/
  2. Preview changes as described above
  3. Commit and push — docs deploy automatically

docs.title: Style
docs.text:
• Use Material alerts
  • Use GitHub Flavored Markdown (tables, code blocks)
  • Keep filenames lowercase with underscores
  • One # heading per file (becomes page title)

docs.title: Installation on HPC
docs.text:
This documentation guides the user on installing COMPSs, and its Python bindings PyCOMPSs. The COMPSs documentation provides already a good overview of the process and the user is advised to read it beforehand to understand what is installed.

PyCOMPSs documentation links
  • Installation overview
  • COMPSs documentation on dependencies
  • COMPSs documentation on HPC installation.

docs.title: [Recommended] Manual installation: example
docs.text:
This installation follows the official one. It shows the main passages as done in the CINECA's cluster Leonardo.

Warning

Please, refer to COMPSs documentation for more info and guidance on your cluster.

We assume that the user is connected to the cluster.

docs.title: 1: Load dependencies
docs.text:
Load the required dependencies. In Leonardo, using modules:

  • Java:

    module load openjdk/11.0.20.1_1

  • Boost:

    module load boost/1.85.0--openmpi--4.1.6--gcc--12.2.0

  • Python:

    module load python/3.11.7

    In Leonardo, you need to install pip and other required building tools for the user. For example:

    python -m ensurepip --upgrade
python -m pip install --user wheel setuptools --upgrade

  • Autotools: usually already available. Testable with autoconf --version.

  • gcc:

    module load gcc/12.2.0

    For more info on gcc compilation, see the Troubleshoot section.

docs.title: 2: Setup environment variables
docs.text:
Make sure the following environment variables are set:

  • JAVA_HOME: should be set by the openjdk module. Check with echo $JAVA_HOME.

  • BOOST_CPPFLAGS: check the one used for the boost library compilation. On Leonardo, inspect $BOOST_HOME/.spack/spack-build-out.txt:

    export BOOST_CPPFLAGS="-std=c++11 -pthread -O2 -s"

    These are the default flags of the B2 building system for that version.

docs.title: 3: Download and install COMPSs
docs.text:
From the download page select the COMPSs version:

wget https://compss.bsc.es/repo/sc/stable/COMPSs_<version>.tar.gz
tar -xvzf COMPSs_<version>.tar.gz
cd COMPSs
./install -T <targetDir> [<supercomputer.cfg>]

Note that supercomputer.cfg refers to the config file used for that HPC and Scheduler (more info on the Configuration section, example files can be found in COMPSs/Runtime/scripts/queues/supercomputers). <targetDir> is where to install COMPSs, be aware that the content of that directory will be erased. -T excludes the tracing system, however it can be included if the supercomputer supports extrae (for more info see the official documentation). More info on the available flags with ./install --help.

A correct installation prints the successful installation of COMPSs and all its bindings to stdout.

docs.title: 4: Create a (tcl) module
docs.text:
To make binaries available and set the right environment variables in the shell, create a tcl module:

touch <path/to/modules>/compss/<version>

A minimal example:

#%Module

set COMPSS_HOME "<targetDir>"
prepend-path PATH "${COMPSS_HOME}/Runtime/scripts/user:${COMPSS_HOME}/Runtime/scripts/utils"
prepend-path CLASSPATH "${COMPSS_HOME}/Runtime/compss-engine.jar"
prepend-path PATH "${COMPSS_HOME}/Bindings/c/bin"
prepend-path PYTHONPATH "${COMPSS_HOME}/Bindings/python/
export R_LIBS_USER=${COMPSS_HOME}/Bindings/RCOMPSs/user_libs/:$R_LIBS_USER

setenv COMPSS_HOME $COMPSS_HOME

prereq python/3.11.7
prereq openjdk/11.0.20.1_1

R_LIBS_USER is used in case of R bindings installation.

Save it in <path/to/modules>/compss/[version] and load it using:

module use --append <path/to/modules> # that can be added in ~/.bashrc or before a workflow run
module load compss/[version]

To test out the installation, after loading the module, run:

enqueue_compss -h

docs.title: Dardel Installation
docs.text:
We use a custom Java 21 JRE installation because of dependencies mismatch with the OpenJDK available in Dardel. Hence, we use the Oracle JRE LTS 21:

cd # perform operation in the user home
wget https://download.oracle.com/java/21/latest/jdk-21_linux-x64_bin.tar.gz
tar -xvf jdk-21_linux-x64_bin.tar.gz
rm jdk-21_linux-x64_bin.tar.gz

The relative lua module saved in <pathToModules>/modules/java/21.lua is:

-- -*- lua -*-
-- Module: jdk
-- -- Sets up Java 21 (JDK 21.0.12.1)

help([[
This module sets up the Java Development Kit (JDK) 21.0.12.1.

It sets JAVA_HOME and adds $JAVA_HOME/bin to PATH.
]])

whatis("Name: JDK")
whatis("Version: 21.0.12.1")
whatis("Description: Java Development Kit")
whatis("Sets JAVA_HOME and prepends $JAVA_HOME/bin to PATH")

local HOME = "<userHomePathAbsolute>/jdk-21.0.12.1"

setenv("JAVA_HOME", HOME)
prepend_path("PATH", pathJoin(HOME, "bin"))

Then we can install COMPSs with:

# Load order might be important
ml PDCOLD/24.11
module use <pathToModules>/modules
ml java/21
ml boost/1.85.0-cpeGNU-24.11
ml all-spack-modules/0.23.1 # required for the following Python version
ml python/3.13.0-gcc-cgo
ml gcc/12.2.0
python -m ensurepip --upgrade
python -m pip install --user wheel setuptools --upgrade

wget https://compss.bsc.es/repo/sc/stable/COMPSs_3.4.tar.gz
tar -xvzf COMPSs_3.4.tar.gz
cd COMPSs
./install -T <proj>/installation/compss_3_4 dardel.cfg

And generated the following Lua module (for the Lmod system) in <pathToModules>/modules/compss/3.4.lua:

-- -*- lua -*-

local compss_home = "<pathToInstallation>/installation/compss_3_4/"

prepend_path("MODULEPATH", "<pathToModules>/modules")

depends_on("PDCOLD/24.11")
depends_on("all-spack-modules/0.23.1")
depends_on("boost/1.85.0-cpeGNU-24.11")
depends_on("python/3.13.0-gcc-cgo")
depends_on("java/21")

source_sh("bash", pathJoin(compss_home, "compssenv"))

setenv("COMPSS_HOME", compss_home)

The Gromacs version tested is gromacs/2026.1-cpeGNU-24.11.

docs.title: [Experimental] Installation using Spack
docs.text:
Warning

This installation is experimental and not directly supported by the COMPSs' Team. If issues arises, please refer to the officially supported manual installation

Spack references
  • Add a package to Spack
  • Advance packaging tutorial
  • Reference files in directory spack

Info

This repository contains two package.py depending on the Spack version. 0_22/compss/package.py has been tested with Spack <= 0.22.x. 1_00/compss/package.py has been tested with Spack 1.0 > <= 1.2.

If you encounter any issues in the process, read the troubleshooting section before open an issue.

These steps assume that Spack is available in your shell. It might be loaded in your HPC environment, for example using module load spack.

If you already have a Spack custom repo (in this example, the namespace is called <repo name>), skip to step 2, otherwise start from 1 creating a custom repo. Custom repos are required because most probably you won't have the permission to add software to the main repo of your cluster.

1. Create a personal repo

spack repo create path/to/root/repos <repo name>
spack repo add path/to/root/repos/<repo name>

This will create a new repository, and a namespace, where to add recipes for softwares called <repo name>.

2. Add COMPSs to the repo

spack create --name compss -N <repo name>

Then you will be prompted with the default editor to update the package.py of COMPSs that you can close. Overwrite the content of spack edit compss with the package.py from this repo:

cp <this repo>/docs/spack/<spack_version>/compss/package.py path/to/root/repos/<repo name>/packages/compss/

3. Install COMPSs

Concretize the spec and install COMPSs, specifying the cfg through the environment variable COMPSS_SUPERCOMPUTER_CFG (only the filename):

spack spec -Il compss

COMPSS_SUPERCOMPUTER_CFG=leonardo.cfg spack install compss

4. Generate the Tcl module

Load environment variables and add binaries to PATH:

spack module tcl refresh -y

Now, load COMPSs in the current shell:

module load compss

The full name will look something like compss/3.3.3--gcc--12.2.0. Alternatively:

spack load compss

To test the installation just type enqueue_compss --version.

docs.title: Troubleshoot
docs.text:
The user cannot create a personal repo in the cluster

If this operation results in permission errors in your cluster, probably the user is not allowed to have a personal repo.yaml file. In this case, contact your system administrator. A possible solution could be re-enable the user to perform such operation specifying unset SPACK_DISABLE_LOCAL_CONFIG

COMPSs cannot be found when creating the Spack spec

In a cluster, is customary to have a system Spack repository called builtin. This can be checked using: 

$ spack repo list
[+] builtin     v2.2    /path/to/builtin
[+] <repo name>    v2.4    /path/to/<repo name>
If builtin is higher than you personal <repo name>, as in the above output, Spack might not find compss because it searches for it in builtins. To solve this, you can specify the namespace from which the package should be installed: 
spack spec -Il <repo name>.compss
and similarly when installing it.

Errors while compiling COMPSs with gcc 13 or later

There are two possibilities. You can unsure that the C compilation is compliant with the COMPSs code by specifying the environmental variable export CFLAGS="-std=gnu17" before installing COMPSs. This is an easy fix with recent gcc versions. You might need to modify the spack recipe in case the variable is not correctly used.

On the other side, one can use gcc 12 by specifying to spack to use it. To ensure this you can specify a compilation preference (for transitive dependencies, because COMPSs does not depend on gcc directly). On Spack 1.0 or later, find Spack's package.yaml with: 

spack config edit packages
and add: 
packages:
  c:
    prefer:
    - gcc@12
  cxx:
    prefer:
    - gcc@12

Cannot install PyCOMPSs because no pip available

In this case, you need to install pip within the Python interpreter that you use to install PyCOMPSs and run workflows. Follow the official documentation for this.

Be aware that if you install pip and PyCOMPSs within a venv, PyCOMPSs will be installed only on that virtual environment. Therefore, you will need to always source it to run a workflow. We discourage the latter approach.

No module compss when using module load

If you cannot find the compss module, you need to issue first (or append to your shell config file, e.g. ~/.bashrc, to make it permanent) module use --append $SPACK_HOME/modules/ or the location where Spack creates modules.

enqueue_compss runs but it cannot find other binaries

If binaries like enqueue_compss or related are in the PATH variable, but do not work when invoked, inspect the module file generated with ml show compss. A common problem is an incorrect COMPSS_HOME environmental variable.

To fix this, you need to modify accordingly to the error the package.py file in the env.set("COMPSS_HOME", compss_home) line.

docs.title: Post-installation configuration
docs.text:
COMPSs uses configuration files to adapt to different clusters. The general structure is the following:

where sc.cfg is the supercomputer config file and queue_system.cfg is the confif file for the job scheduler.

docs.title: Supercomputer
docs.text:
This file is selected during installation when calling ./install or with the env var COMPSS_SUPERCOMPUTER_CFG. Afterward, it is renamed as default.cfg in the COMPSs installation directory (<targetDir>Runtime/scripts/queues/supercomputers/default.cfg or $COMPSS_HOME/Runtime/scripts/queues/supercomputers/default.cfg), where config files for other clusters are.

Supercomputers cfg files contains a set of variables to indicate the queue system used by a supercomputer, paths where the shared disk is mounted, etc. These files are provided with the COMPSs installation, already tuned for different supercomputers by the BSC team. We suggest taking a look at them to have an idea of the default parameters. If not specified in the enqueue_compss flags, the default.cfg one is picked.

For reproducibility, in this repo the cfg files stored in supercomputer_configs are tested to work with the implementation of the md workflow.

docs.title: Queue system (scheduler)
docs.text:
The cfg files contain a set of variables which are used by the other scripts. On one hand, the queue system cfgs contain variables to indicate the commands used by the system to submit and spawn processes, the commands or variables to get the allocated nodes and the directives to indicate the number of nodes, processes, etc. These are container in $COMPSS_HOME/Runtime/scripts/queues/queue_systems/.

The user is advice to not change them.

docs.title: GROMACS
docs.text:
Warning

We strongly suggest to follow the official documentation, the following are demostrations for specific systems that are not necessarly the best configuration for that system

Example of manual installation on Leonardo

The main idea is to have GROMACS relying on installed libraries and softwares to exploit their optimization for the specific cluster.

By loading the cuda module, nvcc will be available to GROMACS. Moreover, cmake is able to find cuFFT from the LD_LIBRARY_PATH.

Procedure:

ml gcc/12.2
ml cuda/12.2
ml openmpi/4.1.6--gcc--12.2.0-cuda-12.2
ml fftw/3.3.10--openmpi--4.1.6--gcc--12.2.0-spack0.22
ml cmake/4.1.2
ml openblas/0.3.26--gcc--12.2.0
ml netlib-scalapack/2.2.0--openmpi--4.1.6--gcc--12.2.0-spack0.22
ml hdf5/1.14.3--openmpi--4.1.6--gcc--12.2.0-spack0.22

tar xfz gromacs-2026.3.tar.gz
cd gromacs-2026.3
mkdir build
cd build
cmake .. -DGMX_MPI=on -DGMX_GPU=CUDA -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX=$PUBLIC/gromacs/gromacs_2026_3 -DGMX_FFT_LIBRARY=fftw3 -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=80 -DREGRESSIONTEST_DOWNLOAD=ON

# entering a Leonardo DCGP compute node
srun -A cin_staff -p dcgp_usr_prod -N1 -n16 -t 02:00:00 --pty /bin/bash
make -j 16
make check -j 16
make install

Then, one needs to prepare a module file in <pathToModules>/gromacs/2026.3, such as:

#%Module

module-whatis "GROMACS is a molecular dynamics package primarily designed for simulations of proteins, lipids and nucleic acids. It was originally developed in the Biophysical Chemistry department of University of Groningen, and is now maintained by contributors in universities and research centers across the world."


proc ModulesHelp { } {
puts stderr "Loads GROMACS 2026.3"
}

set GROMACS_HOME "$PUBLIC/gromacs/gromacs_2026_3"
source-sh bash ${GROMACS_HOME}/bin/GMXRC

prereq gcc
prereq cuda/12.2
prereq openmpi/4.1.6--gcc--12.2.0-cuda-12.2
prereq fftw/3.3.10--openmpi--4.1.6--gcc--12.2.0-spack0.22
prereq openblas/0.3.26--gcc--12.2.0
prereq netlib-scalapack/2.2.0--openmpi--4.1.6--gcc--12.2.0-spack0.22
prereq hdf5/1.14.3--openmpi--4.1.6--gcc--12.2.0-spack0.22

Note that we need to make all the dynamically linked libraries available at runtime. Moreover, we just need to source with source-sh the bash script provided by GROMACS.

docs.title: Quickstart Guide
docs.text: This workflow uses PyCOMPSs as Workflow Managment System and GROMACS with PMX for MD and Free Energy evaluations.

docs.title: 1. Get the repository
docs.text:
Clone this repository where you want to use it:

git clone https://github.com/GANANA-EU-INDIA/WP3-P3-workflow.git
cd WP3-P3-workflow

Optionally, create a branch to keep the original workflow intact and allow future updates via git pull:

git switch -c new-branch-name

docs.title: 2. Install PyCOMPSs on HPC
docs.text:
Info

Full details in PyCOMPSs installation section.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: Java (11+), Boost, Python (3.11+), gcc, autotools. Load via your cluster's module system.

docs.title: Manual installation
docs.text:
wget https://compss.bsc.es/repo/sc/stable/COMPSs_<version>.tar.gz
tar -xvzf COMPSs_<version>.tar.gz
cd COMPSs
./install -T <targetDir> [<supercomputer.cfg>]

Create a TCL module file to expose $COMPSS_HOME, PATH, CLASSPATH, PYTHONPATH. See PyCOMPSs.md for a template.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text: enqueue_compss -h

docs.title: 3. Set up and run the workflow
docs.text:
Info

Full details: workflow setup and usage.

docs.title: Python environment
docs.text:
python -m venv ../envs/<venv_name> --system-site-packages
source ../envs/<venv_name>/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt

--system-site-packages exposes PyCOMPSs to the venv.

docs.title: Gromacs
docs.text: The user is responsible to install Gromacs in the machine. Please refer to the official installation guide or an example for the Leonardo cluster.

docs.title: File structure
docs.text: File Purpose When to edit Makefile Entry point, default arguments Change workflow execution defaults workflow/md.py Task definitions, pipeline logic Adapt workflow steps wrapper/env_config_<cluster>.sh Cluster modules, enqueue_compss flags New cluster or queue settings wrapper/submit_workflow.sh Submission wrapper to enqueue_compss Rarely

docs.title: Submit
docs.text:
make                                # list targets
make md                             # default run
make CLUSTERNAME=dardel NODES=4     # override defaults

Outputs and .COMPSs/ runtime logs appear in the workflow directory.

docs.title: Clean up
docs.text: make clean

docs.title: 4. Contribute back
docs.text:
Info

See more info in the contribution documentation

Made an improvement? Open a Pull Request:

git add -A
git commit -m "Describe your changes"
git push origin feat-branch-name

Then open a PR to the main repository and wait for review.

For bugs or feature requests, open an issue using the provided templates.

docs.title: Tools
docs.text: All tools can be found in tools/.

docs.title: COMPSs Monitor Runner
docs.text:
This document describes the usage of tools/run_compss_monitor.sh

Info

This bash script is based on the COMPSs Monitor Documentation.

Warning

This script might fail due to your system configuration (or OS, currently this works only on Linux/OSX/Unix/WSL). In case of failure, refer to the COMPSs documentation for exploiting this feature (and if you want, open an issuein the repo)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
A convenience script for running the COMPSs Monitor locally by:

  1. Detecting container runtime (Docker/Podman) and pulling the COMPSs image
  2. Mounting the remote .COMPSs directory via SSHFS
  3. Starting the COMPSs Monitor in a Docker container

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Container runtime — Docker or Podman installed and running
  • SSHFS — installed on your system
  • SSH access — must have previously connected to the cluster (host key accepted)

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
In your local machine, when a PyCOMPSs workflow is running remotely, run the script as:

./tools/run_compss_monitor.sh <cluster> <remote_parent_path> [local_path]

Example

./tools/run_compss_monitor.sh leonardo /path/to/work/space/WP3-P3-workflow/md/examples/pdb/output
./tools/run_compss_monitor.sh dardel /home/user/projects ~/compss-logs

Once running, access the monitor at:

http://localhost:8080/compss-monitor

Login: /

If the script is not executable, use chmod +x ./tools/run_compss_monitor.sh.

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Argument Description cluster SSH alias configured in ~/.ssh/config remote_parent_path Remote directory where .COMPSs resides (without /.COMPSs suffix) local_path (optional) Local mount point (default: ~/.COMPSs) --stop Stop the monitor container and unmount SSHFS

docs.title: Stop monitoring
docs.text:
./tools/run_compss_monitor.sh --stop
# or manually:
docker stop compss-monitor   # Container auto-removes on stop
fusermount -u ~/.COMPSs       # Unmount remote directory

docs.title: Setup and usage of md workflow
docs.text: These instructions describe the setup and the usage of the workflow WP3-P3-workflow/md. This can be used directly or as a template for a new workflow.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
This guide assumes that you have PyCOMPSs installed.

  1. Fork this repo: 
    git clone https://github.com/GANANA-EU-INDIA/WP3-P3-md-workflow.git
  2. Setup Python environment
  3. (Optional) Adapt the workflow and configure execution environment
  4. Run the workflow

docs.title: Python environment
docs.text:
Load the same Python that was used to install PyCOMPSs. If you followed the installation, load the compss module with the Python interpreter as dependency. The precise procedure changes from cluster to cluster, it can be as simple as ml compss. Then, create a Python virtual environment using:

python -m venv ../envs/<venv_name> --system-site-packages
. ../envs/<venv_name>/bin/activate

--system-site-packages is fundamental to make the PyCOMPSs package available when the venv is sourced.

Add to the requirements.txt file the Python packages required by your workflow. Then, install them:

python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
uv or conda can be used too.

Info

For more info on how this environment is sourced when submitting a workflow, see md/wrapper/env_config_<cluster>.sh.

docs.title: Submit a workflow
docs.text:
Using default arguments:

make md

Info

Every Python file inside md/workflow can be called by make, just use the script name without .py

Using custom arguments:

make CLUSTERNAME=leonardo NODES=4 INPUT_DIR=./data/inputs

Just type make to have more info or inspect the Makefile.

docs.title: Remove output files
docs.text:
make clean
If you used custom keywords, you might need to specify them.

docs.title: Input directory structure
docs.text:
The workflow expects input directories organized as follows: 

dataset/
├── protein1/
│   ├── structure.pdb
│   ├── select.txt
│   ├── emin-charmm.mdp
│   ├── nvt-charmm.mdp
│   ├── npt-charmm.mdp
│   └── md-charmm.mdp
├── protein2/
│   ├── structure.pdb
│   ├── select.txt
│   ├── emin-charmm.mdp
│   ├── nvt-charmm.mdp
│   ├── npt-charmm.mdp
│   └── md-charmm.mdp
Each protein directory must contain:

  • One PDB file (the input structure)
  • select.txt (selection file for pdb2gmx)
  • MD parameter files: emin-charmm.mdp, nvt-charmm.mdp, npt-charmm.mdp, md-charmm.mdp

See the example directory for more info.

docs.title: Monitor workflow execution
docs.text:
To monitor a running workflow locally, use the COMPSs Monitor Runner. Hence, from your local machine (not the cluster!):

./tools/run_compss_monitor.sh <cluster> <remote_parent_path>
./tools/run_compss_monitor.sh --stop

docs.title: Repository structure
docs.text:
Info

This part refers to the md directory

This repo uses a simplified approach to execute PyCOMPSs workflows. The following table summarizes the role of each file in the workflow definition and execution. Levels represent the order of call when submitting a workflow (or, alternatively, the "distance" between the user issuing make and the workflow definition).

level file description For more info Target 0 Makefile Interface to easily handle workflow submission. Arguments that change often can be passed directly to make type make Wrapper 1 md/wrapper/submit_workflow.sh Wrapper to the enqueue_compss program. type make PyCOMPSs 1 md/wrapper/env_config_<cluster>.sh Configuration file sourced by submit_workflow.sh. This bash describes the shell environment in which the workflow will be executed. Check the file Shell environment, Slurm 2 md/workflow/md.py Tasks and pipeline implementation. This file controls the whole workflow. Check the file Workflow 3 md/workflow/md-provenance.yaml Configuration for Data Provenance. Check the file Workflow

In this setup, the workflow is managed through a Makefile. The arguments that change often (such as input/output directories, number of cores per task, workflow name etc) are passed directly to make while more "stable" arguments are configured in ./wrapper. The main files for the workflow specification are stored inside ./wrapper/env_config_<cluster>.sh and ./wrapper/submit_workflow.sh.

Warning

Currently, not all Slurm or COMPSs arguments are wrapped. To modify this aspect, see how to do it.

All arguments that are not set either in make nor env_config_<cluster>.sh use the default values as expressed in the COMPSs queue config file $COMPSS_HOME/Runtime/scripts/queues/supercomputers/default.cfg. See COMPSs documentation for more info.

docs.title: Miscellaneous notes
docs.text:
Note

These are some notes for version 3.3.3 for edge cases or non-standard behaviors.

  • the bin argument working_dir can lead to problems even if the file passed as arguments of the function are described by absolute paths. The example is using pdb_delhetatom, in which specifying the working dir as the parent to the input and output directories, messes up the paths even though in the main function these are passed as str of the absolute, resolved, path. (still don't know why).
  • the explicitely defined arguments to a binary inside the binary decorator is cleaner, hence it is best practice, than defining arguments through the python function arguments. See md.py.
  • shell scripts can be used to wrap another program/binary that does not a flag/way to specify which and how many files it produces (nor a directory where it outputs).
  • the constraint decorator instruct the task on the OMP threads to allocate for the task, among many other things. This implies that it set the OMP_NUM_THREADS environmental variable that, otherwise, cannot be exported before the enqueue_compss invocation.
  • when using gmx mdrun you should always check the mdp file that starts the simulation to know which file will be produced. A common error is the fact that, if you don't specify the keywords nstxout and similar, you won't get a trajectory file. Only a checkpoint file will be produced. Hence, if in the workflow you specified to output a trr file but it does not appear, COMPSs will exit with an error, causing you headaches.
  • COMPSs search for checkpoints and loads them! It avoids running the same task multiple times
  • you have to pass to the enqueue_compss the checkpoint related flags, specifically checkpoint_folder.
  • you can run the workflow one time configuring checkpoints. When you run it again with the same checkpoint folder config you'll see in the runtime.log (inside .COMPSs dir) the loading of the checkpoints.
  • in the summary, obtained through the --summary flag, you can see that in the second run no computations are performed.
  • one unresolved issues (as in the 3.3.3 version): in the second identical run, the runtime waits indefinetly with the line [LAUNCH_COMPSS] Waiting for application completion in compss-[id-job].out.
  • print statements in the main code that write on the STOUT, are catched by the .COMPSs/jobs/job-[JOBID].out files.

docs.title: Adapt the workflow at your needs
Adapt the workflow
docs.text:
Typically, one starts modifying the Python scripts in workflow in which a high-level description of the workflow divided in tasks is detailed. After that, one specifies the environment in which the workflow will be executed. The latter is controlled by bash scripts in wrapper and the Makefile.

The procedure is usually the following:

  1. Workflow definition: define a Python script controlling the main pipeline. The tasks involved in the workflow can be defined in the same file or in separate ones. All these are stored in workflow. The main Python file has a name that will be used to call PyCOMPSs. In this repo, tasks and pipeline are detailed inside md/workflow/md.py. Hence, the name of the workflow is md.
  2. Setup the execution environment: open md/wrapper/env_config_<cluster>.sh and customize Slurm variables, modules to load before execution and everything to prepare the shell for workflow execution. This bash is sourced before launching enqueue_compss, which is called in md/wrapper/submit_workflow.sh. Customize the latter to adjust enqueue_compss flags.
Some references to get started with PyCOMPSs

  • PyCOMPSs application development

docs.title: Add more Slurm or COMPSs arguments to the wrappers
docs.text:
Example on how to modify level <= 1 (see table): implement a new COMPSs argument. Firstly, decide whether the argument has to be specified at the Makefile level or at the env_config_<cluster>.sh level. In the two cases:

Makefile

  1. Update the Makefile adding the argument on top and on the wrapper call
  2. Modify submit_workflow.sh to catch the new argument from the command line (attention to the sanity checks), add description and add it to the other variables
  3. In the same file, add the argument to the enqueue_compss call

env_config_<cluster>.sh

  1. Update the file in the relevant section
  2. In submit_workflow.sh, add the argument to the enqueue_compss call
